Ground truth survey was carried out to authenticate as well as measure the accuracy of
SCS-CN method for larger watershed (>15 km2). As depicted in Fig. 9, the farm pond

ponds were identified, out of which four were existing and 12 were potential site. As study
area shows moderate to high runoff, 40 check dams were identified at the first to third order
stream along soil type C, while nine potential sites were identified. Check dams are
recommended across the 2nd and 3rd order streams, with low to moderate slopes.

retained_profile.source_weight: No numeric stream-order weight reported for the intersection of these per-structure specifications.
retained_profile.scope: Upper Karha, semi-arid basaltic western India. Table 6/PDF14 is an adopted specification. PDF12 specifically recommends orders 2 and 3 for check dams on low to moderate slopes. Field account describes farm ponds on first order, check dams across orders 1–3, existing percolation tanks on fourth order, and gully plugs on first order (PDF12–13). No ordinal score or optimal second-order response is assigned by Table 6.
retained_profile.network_definition: Methods PDF4 name Horton (1945) stream ordering for a toposheet-derived drainage map updated with satellite data and DEM/ArcSWAT. Current EV says Strahler. Retain the actual source designation and defer any equivalence until network and algorithm are established.
retained_profile.lineage: Adopted IMSD (1995) specifications, explicitly attributed below Table 6. Study checked local siting in the field. Distinguish adopted conditions, local advice and observed placements.

claims.source_review_note: Kadam et al. (2012), Table 6/PDF14, adopts IMSD (1995) criteria. Farm ponds and gully plugs use order 1. Check dams and percolation tanks allow orders 1–4 with different slopes, runoff and soils. PDF12 recommends orders 2 and 3 for check dams on low to moderate slopes and reports check dams on orders 1–3. Methods PDF4 name Horton ordering, while the EV calls it Strahler. Keep each structure and each kind of evidence identifiable.
claims.dashboard_reason: Next mapping review — runoff-catchment stream order. Kadam et al., Table 6 (PDF p. 14), adopt order 1 for farm ponds and gully plugs and orders 1–4 for check dams and percolation tanks. For check dams, p. 12 recommends orders 2–3 on low-to-moderate slopes and identifies check dams on orders 1–3 during field verification. Page 4 cites Horton for stream ordering. The current evidence record labels the order Strahler. Check the ordering method before matching a network.

supporting_native_excerpts.locator: cached PDF page 12; native text slice
supporting_native_excerpts.quote:
Suitability criteria used for identifying RWH zones and
sites for farm ponds, percolation tanks and check dams were
adopted from the literature (Chowdary et al., 2009; Jha et al., 2014)
and are summarized in Table 6. Farm ponds are planned in agri-
cultural land, whereas percolation tanks are planned in the
wasteland and degraded forest areas. For identifying suitable lo-
cations for percolation tanks and check dams, a drainage network
map of the study area with a 50-m buffer around 2nd and 3rd order
streams was generated in the GIS environment.

supporting_native_excerpts.locator: cached PDF page 14; native text slice
supporting_native_excerpts.quote:
Drainage network map of the study area was derived from SRTM
DEM using ArcHydro of ArcGIS software. Drainage order in the
study area is found to be of 4th order (Fig. 10), with the total
drainage length of 2341 km. Nearly 47% of the drainage network is
of the ﬁrst order, while the second and third order streams, which
are important for in-stream RWH/recharge structures, cover 29 and
19%, respectively.

The older Singh EV context describes intake as pending. Count as shared lineage. Jha uses light-textured percolation soil; Singh prints coarse textured. No cross-source replacement.

The table cites Jha (2014), now registered separately with shared lineage.

model building is the digital elevation model (DEM) of 30 m

ASTGTM2_N32W006, ASTGTM2_N32W007, ASTGTM2_

supporting_native_excerpts.quote:
With the hydrology 
tools available in ArcGIS software, the drainage density and 
the stream order, according to the Horton and Strahler clas-
sifications (Horton 1945; Strahler 1952, 1964), are automati-
cally assessed based on flow accumulation data derived from 
DEM.

supporting_native_excerpts.locator: cached PDF page 6; native text slice
supporting_native_excerpts.quote:
Another consideration is that streams of 
order 1 are undesirable and are assigned score 0, while suit-
ability decreases with the stream order. Streams of third and 
fourth orders can be suitable for small check dam construc-
tion (Pophare and Balparde 2014). Streams of higher orders 
receive higher runoff volumes, resulting in an increased risk 
of dam collapse (Nyssen et al. 2006). Therefore, streams of 
sixth order and higher are considered non-suitable.

retained_profile.scope: Check-dam site selection for Khenifra, Morocco. Table 1/PDF6 ranks stream orders by susceptibility to accumulate surface water. Order 1 receives 0. The EV currently omits it. The table assigns order ≥6 score 1 (“Very low”), confirmed numerically in PDF7; explanatory prose PDF6 calls ≥6 non-suitable. Preserve the disagreement.

source_weight.locator: Eq.7 and Table 2, PDF7. CR reported PDF12.

retained_profile.network_definition: PDF5 describes a 30 m ASTER DEM, GIS flow accumulation, and Horton and Strahler classifications. Source ranking depends on this network.
retained_profile.validation: Source reports validation for the full multi-factor map against depressions at different depths (PDF7 and 12). This evaluates site mapping for water accumulation. It supplies no independent calibration of the individual stream-order categories or structural safety.
retained_profile.lineage: PDF6 cites Pophare & Balparde (2014) for orders 3/4 and Nyssen et al. (2006) for collapse risk at higher flow. Do not attribute the complete 0–5 score table to these references. The reported scores and 0.10 weight belong to Ettazarini’s model.

claims.source_review_note: Ettazarini (2021), Table 1/PDF6, scores check-dam stream orders 1→0, 2→5, 3→4, 4→3, 5→2, ≥6→1. The EV omits order 1. The paper calls ≥6 non-suitable in the prose and very low (1) in the table. Eq.7/Table 2 gives stream order an AHP weight of 0.10. The current shared upper bound of 4 discards ranked orders 5 and above.
